subject: Geography
practicalPaper: Paper 3 (Elements of Practical and Physical Geography) lasts 1 hour 50 minutes for 70 marks: candidates answer four of eight questions, including the compulsory Question 1 on reading and interpreting a topographical map (25 marks); the others (15 marks each) cover statistical diagrams, weather and climate data, rocks and physical geography. Field work on local geography is examined by schools as part of continuous assessment.

practicals.title: Map scales: types and conversion
practicals.aim: To recognise the three ways of showing a map scale (statement, representative fraction and linear scale) and convert from one form to another.
apparatus: Topographical map sheets with different scales
safety: Handle maps carefully and avoid folding them along new lines.
procedure: Locate the scale in the margin of the map and identify how it is shown.
To convert a statement (e.g. 1 cm to 0.5 km) to a representative fraction (RF), express both sides in the same unit: 0.5 km = 50 000 cm, so RF = 1:50 000.
To convert an RF to a statement, divide the denominator by 100 000 to get kilometres per centimetre.
To draw a linear scale, choose a convenient length (e.g. 10 cm), work out the ground distance it represents and divide it into equal primary divisions.
Divide the left-hand primary division into smaller secondary divisions and label 0 at the junction.
Label the scale with units and the RF.
practicals.expectedObservations: Large-scale maps (e.g. 1:25 000) show small areas in great detail; small-scale maps (e.g. 1:1 000 000) show large areas with little detail.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Statement 1 cm to 2.5 km: 2.5 km = 250 000 cm → RF 1:250 000.
RF 1:50 000 → 50 000 cm = 0.5 km, so 1 cm represents 0.5 km (2 cm to 1 km).
Linear scale for 1:50 000: a 10 cm line represents 10 × 0.5 = 5 km; mark primary divisions every 2 cm (1 km) and divide the first 2 cm into 5 parts of 200 m.
precautions: Always convert to the same unit before writing an RF.
Begin the linear scale with 0 between the primary and secondary divisions.
Use a sharp pencil.
sourcesOfError: Inaccurate division of the linear scale.
commonMistakes: Writing RF with units, e.g. 1 cm : 50 000 cm.
Calling 1:1 000 000 a large scale.
Placing 0 at the far left of the linear scale.
examTips: Show each conversion step; marks are given for method.
Remember: 1 km = 1000 m = 100 000 cm.

checkQuestions.q: A scale of 1 cm to 5 km written as an RF is
On a 1:25 000 map, 1 cm represents
Which is the largest scale?
checkQuestions.explanation: The smaller the denominator, the larger the scale.

practicals.title: Measuring straight and curved distances on a map
practicals.aim: To measure straight-line (as the crow flies) and curved distances (roads, rivers, railways) on a topographical map and convert them to ground distances.
apparatus: Topographical map (e.g. 1:50 000 sheet of part of Nigeria or West Africa)
materials: Strip of paper with a straight edge
safety: Use dividers carefully; their points are sharp.
procedure: For a straight distance, place a ruler between the two points and read the length in cm.
For a curved route, place the straight edge of a paper strip at the starting point and mark it.
Pivot the paper at each bend, marking the paper where the route changes direction, until the end point is reached.
Alternatively, lay a thread along the route, mark the end and straighten it against a ruler.
Measure the total length on the paper or thread.
Convert to ground distance using the scale, or lay the paper against the linear scale directly.
practicals.expectedObservations: Curved routes such as roads and rivers are longer on the ground than the straight-line distance between their ends; the ratio indicates how winding the route is.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Scale 1:50 000 (1 cm = 0.5 km).
Straight distance between two settlements = 7.4 cm → 7.4 × 0.5 = 3.7 km.
Road distance between them = 12.6 cm → 12.6 × 0.5 = 6.3 km.
Sinuosity = 6.3 ÷ 3.7 ≈ 1.70, so the road is about 70% longer than the direct line.
precautions: Mark the paper strip carefully at each bend.
Start and end at the exact points named in the question (e.g. the centre of a settlement or a road junction).
Use small straight segments on very winding routes.
sourcesOfError: Slipping of the paper strip at bends.
commonMistakes: Giving an answer in cm instead of km.
Measuring from the edge of a settlement instead of the point stated.
Using the wrong scale for the map.
examTips: WAEC allows a small tolerance (often ±0.1 to 0.2 km); show your measured map distance as well as the ground distance.
State the answer in the unit requested, usually km.

checkQuestions.q: A road measures 9.2 cm on a 1:50 000 map. The ground distance is
The best simple method of measuring a winding river on a map is
options: the paper-strip method or a thread
a straight ruler from source to mouth
checkQuestions.explanation: Paper strip or thread follows the bends.

checkQuestions.q: On a 1:100 000 map a distance of 3.5 cm represents
checkQuestions.explanation: 1 cm = 1 km at this scale.

practicals.title: Direction and bearing
practicals.aim: To determine the direction (cardinal points) and whole-circle bearing of one point from another on a map, and to calculate back bearings.
apparatus: Topographical map (e.g. 1:50 000 sheet of part of Nigeria or West Africa)
safety: Keep the protractor and dividers in the geometry set when not in use.
procedure: Draw a north–south line through the starting point parallel to the grid eastings (grid north).
Join the starting point to the destination with a straight pencil line.
Place the protractor centre on the starting point with 0° on north.
Measure the angle clockwise from north to the line; this is the bearing, written with three figures (e.g. 065°).
State the direction using the 16 points of the compass.
Calculate the back bearing by adding or subtracting 180°.
practicals.expectedObservations: Bearings range from 000° to 360°; a point exactly north-east has a bearing of 045°, south-west 225°.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Bearing of B from A = 065° (direction ENE).
Back bearing (A from B) = 065° + 180° = 245° (WSW).
Bearing of C from A = 300°; back bearing = 300° − 180° = 120°.
precautions: Always measure clockwise from north.
Draw the north line through the point you are measuring FROM.
Write bearings with three digits.
commonMistakes: Measuring from the wrong point (bearing of A from B instead of B from A).
Measuring anticlockwise.
Writing 65° instead of 065°.
examTips: Read the question wording carefully: 'the bearing of X from Y' means stand at Y.
Allow your answer to fall within the expected range by measuring accurately with a sharp pencil.

checkQuestions.q: The bearing of a point due south-east is
checkQuestions.explanation: SE lies midway between E (090°) and S (180°).

checkQuestions.q: If the bearing of Q from P is 210°, the bearing of P from Q is
Bearings are measured
checkQuestions.explanation: Whole-circle bearings run clockwise from north.

practicals.title: Grid references and measuring area
practicals.aim: To locate features with four- and six-figure grid references and to estimate the area of a feature by counting grid squares.
apparatus: Topographical map (e.g. 1:50 000 sheet of part of Nigeria or West Africa)
safety: Handle tracing paper and maps with clean, dry hands.
procedure: Read the easting (vertical line number) to the left of the feature first, then the northing (horizontal line number) below it: 'along the corridor, then up the stairs'.
For a six-figure reference, divide the square into tenths and estimate the position in each direction.
To find an area, outline the feature (e.g. a forest reserve) on tracing paper over the grid.
Count the complete squares inside the outline.
Count the part squares and divide by 2 (or estimate each part).
Multiply the total number of squares by the ground area of one square.
practicals.expectedObservations: Each grid square on a 1:50 000 sheet with 2 cm grid lines represents 1 km × 1 km = 1 km² on the ground.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
A church is 4 tenths east of easting 23 and 7 tenths north of northing 58 → six-figure reference 234587.
Area of a forest: 14 complete squares + 10 part squares → 14 + 10 ÷ 2 = 19 squares; each square = 1 km² → area ≈ 19 km².
precautions: Always give eastings before northings.
Use the grid line to the left and below the feature.
Count part squares consistently.
sourcesOfError: Irregular outlines making part squares hard to judge.
commonMistakes: Reversing eastings and northings.
Using the line to the right or above the feature.
Forgetting the area unit km².
examTips: Give the six-figure reference exactly as six digits without spaces or commas unless the map uses letters.
Show the counting method for area to earn method marks.

checkQuestions.q: In a grid reference the first figures are the
checkQuestions.explanation: Eastings (read along) come first.

checkQuestions.q: A feature covers 8 whole squares and 6 part squares of 1 km² each. Its approximate area is
On a 1:50 000 map, a grid square with sides of 2 cm represents
checkQuestions.explanation: 2 cm = 1 km on each side, so 1 km².

practicals.title: Map reduction and enlargement
practicals.aim: To reduce or enlarge part of a map using the square (grid) method and calculate the new scale and area.
safety: No special hazards; keep work area tidy.
procedure: Draw a frame around the map area to be copied and divide it into squares (e.g. 2 cm).
For reduction to half, draw a frame with sides half as long and divide it into the same number of squares (1 cm).
Copy the detail in each square into the corresponding small square, noting where lines cross the square edges.
Calculate and write the new RF and draw a new linear scale.
Add a title, north arrow and key.
practicals.expectedObservations: The copied map has the same shape and relative positions of features, but linear dimensions are halved (reduction) or doubled (enlargement).
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Original 1:50 000. Reduced to half (linear): new RF = 1:(50 000 × 2) = 1:100 000. A frame 12 cm × 8 cm becomes 6 cm × 4 cm. Area on paper becomes (1/2)² = 1/4 of the original (96 cm² → 24 cm²).
Enlarged twice: new RF = 1:25 000; the area on paper becomes 4 times larger.
precautions: Use exactly the same number of squares in both frames.
Draw faint construction lines that can be erased.
Transfer details square by square.
commonMistakes: Halving the area instead of the length.
Writing the reduced scale as 1:25 000.
Omitting the title, key, scale or north arrow.
examTips: State the new scale both as an RF and as a linear scale.
Neatness and accuracy of detail transfer earn marks.

checkQuestions.q: A 1:50 000 map reduced to one-half linear size has a scale of
checkQuestions.explanation: Halving the map doubles the denominator.

checkQuestions.q: If the linear size is halved, the area on paper becomes
checkQuestions.explanation: Area scales with the square of the linear factor.

practicals.title: Identifying relief features from contours
practicals.aim: To identify relief features (hill, ridge, spur, valley, saddle, escarpment, plateau, plain, conical hill) from contour patterns on a topographical map.
apparatus: Topographical map (e.g. 1:50 000 sheet of part of Nigeria or West Africa)
safety: No special hazards.
procedure: Find the contour interval from the map margin or by comparing two labelled contours.
Note the values of contours to find which way the land slopes.
Look for patterns: closed rings (hills), V-shapes pointing uphill (valleys), V-shapes pointing downhill (spurs), contours close together (steep slope).
Identify each feature, give its grid reference and its height.
Draw a simple contour sketch of a spur and a valley side by side and label them.
practicals.expectedObservations: Closely spaced contours show steep slopes; widely spaced contours show gentle slopes. Concentric closed contours with the highest in the centre show a hill; a gap between two hills on a ridge shows a saddle (col). Contours bunched on one side and widely spaced on the other show an escarpment.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Contour interval: two labelled contours 300 m and 400 m with four intervals between them → interval = (400 − 300) ÷ 4 = 25 m.
Height of a spot between the 350 m and 375 m contours, halfway → about 362.5 m (≈ 363 m).
precautions: Check contour values before deciding direction of slope.
Use spot heights and trigonometrical stations to confirm summits.
sourcesOfError: Confusing spurs and valleys where no rivers are shown.
commonMistakes: Calling a V pointing downhill a valley — that is a spur.
Ignoring the contour interval.
Naming features without giving their location.
examTips: Rivers flow in valleys; V-shapes of contours along rivers point upstream.
Support each identification with evidence from the map (contour values, grid references).

checkQuestions.q: Contour V-shapes pointing towards higher ground indicate a
checkQuestions.explanation: Valleys cut back into high ground.

checkQuestions.q: Contours very close together indicate
checkQuestions.explanation: Height changes rapidly over a short distance.

checkQuestions.q: Labelled contours of 200 m and 300 m have four gaps between them. The contour interval is
A low point on a ridge between two hills is a
checkQuestions.explanation: A saddle or col lies between two summits.

practicals.title: Calculating gradient
practicals.aim: To calculate the average gradient between two points on a topographical map and express it as a ratio and as an angle.
apparatus: Topographical map (e.g. 1:50 000 sheet of part of Nigeria or West Africa)
safety: No special hazards.
procedure: Find the heights of the two points from contours or spot heights.
Calculate the vertical interval (VI) = difference in height in metres.
Measure the map distance between the points and convert to horizontal equivalent (HE) in metres.
Gradient = VI ÷ HE, expressed as 1 in (HE ÷ VI).
If required, find the angle of slope as tan⁻¹(VI ÷ HE).
practicals.expectedObservations: Steeper slopes give a smaller number in '1 in x' (e.g. 1 in 5 is steeper than 1 in 20).
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Point X = 450 m, Point Y = 200 m → VI = 250 m.
Map distance = 5.0 cm on 1:50 000 → HE = 5.0 × 500 m = 2500 m.
Gradient = 250 ÷ 2500 = 1/10, i.e. 1 in 10.
Angle = tan⁻¹(0.1) ≈ 5.7°.
precautions: Convert VI and HE to the same unit (metres).
Measure the straight-line distance between the exact points.
commonMistakes: Leaving HE in km while VI is in m.
Writing the gradient upside down (10 in 1).
Using the contour interval as the VI.
examTips: Present the formula, substitution and answer as '1 in ...'; each line earns marks.
Round the final ratio sensibly (e.g. 1 in 10, not 1 in 10.0003).

checkQuestions.q: VI = 100 m and HE = 2 km. The gradient is
Which gradient is steepest?
checkQuestions.explanation: A smaller HE per unit rise means steeper.

practicals.title: Drawing a cross profile and testing inter-visibility
practicals.aim: To draw an accurate cross profile (section) between two points on a contour map, calculate vertical exaggeration and determine whether the points are inter-visible.
apparatus: Topographical map (e.g. 1:50 000 sheet of part of Nigeria or West Africa)
safety: No special hazards.
procedure: Join the two points with a faint straight line on the map.
Lay the straight edge of a paper strip along the line and mark the ends, every contour crossed (with its value), rivers, roads and hilltops.
Draw a horizontal base line on graph paper the same length as the strip.
Choose a vertical scale (e.g. 1 cm to 50 m) and draw a vertical axis with heights.
Transfer each mark and plot its height above the base line.
Join the points with a smooth freehand curve, label features and give a title, scales and vertical exaggeration.
Draw a straight line from the start to the end point to test inter-visibility.
practicals.expectedObservations: The profile shows the shape of the land, e.g. steep slopes and valleys. If any ground rises above the line of sight between the two points, they are not inter-visible.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Horizontal scale 1:50 000 (1 cm = 500 m). Vertical scale 1 cm to 50 m = 1:5000.
Vertical exaggeration = horizontal scale denominator ÷ vertical scale denominator = 50 000 ÷ 5000 = 10 times.
Inter-visibility: points at 300 m and 250 m, 6 km apart; a ridge of 320 m lies 2 km from the 300 m point. Line of sight height at 2 km = 300 − (50 × 2 ÷ 6) ≈ 283 m < 320 m, so the points are not inter-visible.
precautions: Keep the vertical scale reasonable (exaggeration about 5–10).
Draw a smooth curve, not straight lines between points.
Remember the profile continues the trend beyond the highest contour on a hilltop.
commonMistakes: Flat-topping hills at the highest contour.
Omitting title, scales and vertical exaggeration.
Joining points with a ruler.
examTips: Marks are given for correct base length, vertical scale, plotting, smooth curve, labels and vertical exaggeration.
State clearly whether the points are inter-visible and give the reason.

checkQuestions.q: Horizontal scale 1:50 000 and vertical scale 1:2500 give a vertical exaggeration of
Two points are not inter-visible if
options: they are at the same height
they are more than 5 km apart
high ground rises above the line joining them on the profile
checkQuestions.explanation: Intervening high ground blocks the line of sight.

checkQuestions.q: Points on a profile should be joined with
checkQuestions.explanation: Land surfaces are smooth curves.

practicals.title: Drainage characteristics and patterns
practicals.aim: To describe the drainage of a mapped area: river direction, patterns (dendritic, trellis, radial, parallel, rectangular), features and drainage density.
apparatus: Topographical map (e.g. 1:50 000 sheet of part of Nigeria or West Africa)
safety: No special hazards.
procedure: Trace the main river and its tributaries.
Use contours to decide the direction of flow (rivers flow from high to low ground).
Identify the drainage pattern from the arrangement of tributaries.
Note features: confluences, meanders, waterfalls, rapids, swamps, dams, wide or narrow valleys.
Measure the total length of all streams with a thread and calculate drainage density.
Describe the drainage in a short paragraph with grid references.
practicals.expectedObservations: A dendritic pattern looks like the branches of a tree and forms on uniform rocks; radial patterns flow outwards from a central hill; trellis patterns have tributaries joining at right angles in areas of alternating hard and soft rock.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Total stream length in an area of 24 km² = 72 cm on 1:50 000 → 72 × 0.5 = 36 km.
Drainage density = 36 km ÷ 24 km² = 1.5 km per km².
precautions: Use contours, not only the map orientation, to decide flow direction.
Include all streams in the area for drainage density.
sourcesOfError: Seasonal streams shown inconsistently on the map.
commonMistakes: Saying rivers flow north because north is at the top of the map.
Naming a pattern without describing evidence.
Listing features without grid references.
examTips: Organise answers: direction of flow, pattern, main river and tributaries, features with grid references, valley shape.
Use the key to confirm features such as waterfalls and swamps.

checkQuestions.q: A tree-like arrangement of tributaries is a
checkQuestions.explanation: Dendritic means tree-like.

checkQuestions.q: Streams flowing outwards in all directions from a hill form a
checkQuestions.explanation: Radial drainage spreads from a central high point.

checkQuestions.q: Total stream length 20 km in an area of 16 km² gives a drainage density of

practicals.title: Settlement, communication and land-use patterns on a map
practicals.aim: To describe and explain patterns of settlement, communication and land use on a topographical map and relate them to relief and drainage.
apparatus: Topographical map (e.g. 1:50 000 sheet of part of Nigeria or West Africa)
safety: No special hazards.
procedure: Identify settlements and classify them as nucleated, dispersed or linear using the key.
Note the sites of settlements (river banks, road junctions, gentle slopes, hilltops).
Identify communication routes (roads, tracks, railways, footpaths) and their alignment with relief.
Identify land uses: farming, forest reserves, plantations, quarrying, markets, schools, churches, mosques.
Count settlements in sample squares and calculate density.
Write explanations linking patterns to relief, drainage and human activities.
practicals.expectedObservations: Settlements often cluster along roads and rivers and avoid steep slopes and swamps; roads follow valleys and gentle slopes; forest reserves occupy steep or hilly land.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Settlement density: 18 settlements in 12 km² of lowland → 1.5 per km²; 2 settlements in 8 km² of upland → 0.25 per km².
Lowland density is 1.5 ÷ 0.25 = 6 times that of the upland.
precautions: Use the key to confirm symbols.
Refer to specific places with grid references.
sourcesOfError: Out-of-date maps may not show recent growth.
Symbols for small settlements may be missed.
commonMistakes: Describing without explaining.
Mixing up settlement pattern (shape) and settlement site (location).
Ignoring evidence from the map.
examTips: Answers must refer to evidence on the map provided (names, grid references, symbols).
Relate human features to physical features: 'the road follows the valley of River X to avoid steep slopes'.

checkQuestions.q: Settlements arranged along a road form a
checkQuestions.explanation: Linear settlements follow a line such as a road or river.

checkQuestions.q: Roads on a map tend to avoid
checkQuestions.explanation: Construction is difficult and costly on steep or swampy land.

practicals.title: Bar graphs and line graphs
practicals.aim: To represent geographical data with simple, compound (divided) and multiple bar graphs and line graphs, and to choose the appropriate type.
materials: Data table, e.g. crop production by state or monthly rainfall
safety: No special hazards.
procedure: Study the data and decide whether it is discrete categories (bar graph) or a continuous series over time (line graph).
Choose a scale that uses most of the graph paper; start the value axis at zero for bar graphs.
Draw and label both axes with units.
Draw bars of equal width with equal gaps (or plot points and join them for a line graph).
For a compound bar, divide each bar into its components in the same order and shade with a key.
Add a title, scale and key.
practicals.expectedObservations: Bar graphs make comparisons between places or items easy; line graphs show trends over time such as rising or falling production.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Cocoa output (thousand tonnes): 2019: 250, 2020: 270, 2021: 280, 2022: 260, 2023: 290.
Mean = 1350 ÷ 5 = 270 thousand tonnes. Percentage change 2019–2023 = (290 − 250) ÷ 250 × 100 = 16%.
Scale: 1 cm to 20 thousand tonnes → the 290 bar is 14.5 cm high.
Compound bar: a state producing 400 t (maize 240, yam 100, cassava 60) has segments of 240, 100 and 60 on a bar of total height 400.
precautions: Use equal bar widths and gaps.
Choose a suitable scale and state it.
Keep the order of components the same in every compound bar.
sourcesOfError: Inaccurate plotting due to awkward scales.
commonMistakes: Starting the vertical axis above zero on a bar graph, which exaggerates differences.
No title, key or units.
Joining points on a bar graph.
examTips: WAEC marks: title, scale, labelled axes, accurate plotting, key/shading, and neatness.
Be ready to state one advantage and one disadvantage of the method.

checkQuestions.q: Data showing change in rainfall over 12 months is best shown with a
checkQuestions.explanation: Monthly data form a time series.

checkQuestions.q: Values 40, 60 and 80 have a mean of
With a scale of 1 cm to 25 units, a bar for 175 units is

practicals.title: Pie charts and proportional circles
practicals.aim: To draw pie charts to show proportions of a total and proportional circles to compare totals between places.
materials: Data table, e.g. land use of a local government area, population of towns
safety: Handle the compass point carefully.
procedure: Total the data.
Calculate each sector angle: value ÷ total × 360°.
Draw a circle, draw a starting radius at 12 o'clock and measure sectors clockwise from largest to smallest.
Shade sectors and add a key, title and percentages.
For proportional circles, calculate the square root of each total.
Choose a scale for the radius and draw each circle with radius proportional to the square root.
practicals.expectedObservations: The size of each sector shows its share of the whole; proportional circles let the reader compare totals by area.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Land use (ha): farmland 450, forest 270, settlement 150, other 30. Total = 900.
Angles: farmland 450 ÷ 900 × 360 = 180°; forest 108°; settlement 60°; other 12° (sum 360°).
Proportional circles: Town A 400 000 people, Town B 100 000. √400 000 ≈ 632.5, √100 000 ≈ 316.2. If B has a radius of 1.0 cm, A has 632.5 ÷ 316.2 = 2.0 cm.
precautions: Check that angles add up to 360°.
Use square roots (not raw values) for proportional circle radii.
Draw sectors in a consistent order with a key.
commonMistakes: Making circle radius directly proportional to the value (this greatly exaggerates large values).
Angles that do not total 360°.
Missing key.
examTips: Show a table of calculated angles before drawing.
State one advantage (clear comparison of parts of a whole) and one disadvantage (hard to compare small sectors).

checkQuestions.q: A value of 30 out of a total of 120 gives a pie-chart angle of
The radius of a proportional circle is proportional to the
checkQuestions.explanation: The area then represents the value.

practicals.title: Dot maps, density (choropleth) maps and isopleth maps
practicals.aim: To show the distribution of data on maps using dots, shaded density classes and lines joining places of equal value.
apparatus: Outline map of an area (e.g. states or local government areas)
materials: Data tables of population, area and values at points (e.g. rainfall)
safety: No special hazards.
procedure: Dot map: choose a dot value (e.g. 1 dot = 5000 people), calculate the number of dots for each area and place them where the feature actually occurs.
Density (choropleth) map: calculate density = value ÷ area for each region.
Group densities into 4–5 classes and choose a graded shading scheme from light (low) to dark (high).
Shade each region and add a key.
Isopleth map: plot point values, choose an interval and draw smooth lines through places of equal value by interpolating between points.
practicals.expectedObservations: Dot maps show where things are concentrated; choropleth maps show average density per area; isopleths show gradual change, e.g. rainfall decreasing northwards in Nigeria.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Dot map: 1 dot = 5000 people. An area with 85 000 people needs 85 000 ÷ 5000 = 17 dots.
Density: a state with 2 400 000 people and 12 000 km² → 2 400 000 ÷ 12 000 = 200 persons/km².
Isopleth interpolation: stations 20 km apart record 1200 mm and 1400 mm; the 1300 mm isohyet passes halfway, 10 km from each.
precautions: Use dots of equal size.
Use a graded shading that gets darker with higher values.
Interpolate proportionally between points.
sourcesOfError: Choice of dot value or class intervals can change the visual impression.
commonMistakes: Spreading dots evenly over an area regardless of where people live.
Random colours for choropleth classes.
Crossing isopleths.
examTips: Explain why the dot value was chosen (avoid too many or too few dots).
Give an advantage and disadvantage of each method.

Lines joining places with equal rainfall are called
checkQuestions.explanation: Isohyets are isopleths of rainfall.

practicals.title: Flow charts and flow maps
practicals.aim: To show movement of goods, people or traffic with flow lines whose width is proportional to the quantity moved, and to draw a flow chart of a process.
materials: Traffic count data or trade data
Process description (e.g. groundnut to oil and cake)
safety: No special hazards.
procedure: Choose a scale for line width, e.g. 1 mm = 1000 vehicles per day.
Calculate the width of each flow line.
Draw the lines along the actual routes with arrows showing direction.
Add a key showing the width scale.
For a flow chart, arrange boxes showing stages of a process and join them with arrows.
practicals.expectedObservations: Wide bands show major routes, e.g. Lagos–Ibadan Expressway carries much more traffic than rural roads.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Scale 1 mm = 1000 vehicles/day. Route A: 12 000 vehicles → 12 mm; Route B: 4500 → 4.5 mm; Route C: 800 → 0.8 mm (shown as a thin line).
Percentage of total on Route A = 12 000 ÷ (12 000 + 4500 + 800) × 100 = 12 000 ÷ 17 300 × 100 ≈ 69.4%.
precautions: Choose a scale so the largest band does not cover the map.
Show direction with arrows.
commonMistakes: Lines not proportional to values.
Missing scale key for widths.
examTips: State the scale used and show calculations of widths.
A flow chart for a process must be in the correct sequence with arrows.

checkQuestions.q: With a scale of 1 mm = 500 tonnes, a flow of 3000 tonnes is drawn
In a flow map, the width of a line represents
checkQuestions.explanation: Width is proportional to volume of flow.

checkQuestions.q: Flow maps are most suitable for showing
checkQuestions.explanation: They show movement along routes.

practicals.title: GIS: building map layers and measuring area
practicals.aim: To understand GIS components and data by creating simple layers (roads, settlements, land use) from a map or satellite image using free GIS or online mapping software, and to calculate area from raster cells.
apparatus: Free GIS software (e.g. QGIS) or an online mapping tool
materials: Scanned topographical map or satellite image of the school area
Table of GPS points collected around the school
safety: Follow computer room rules; keep liquids away from equipment.
When collecting GPS points outside, stay within the school compound with permission.
procedure: Identify the five components of GIS available: hardware, software, data, procedures and people.
Load the scanned map or satellite image as a base layer (raster data).
Create a point layer and add GPS points of buildings, gates and the borehole.
Digitise roads as a line layer and the sports field as a polygon layer (vector data).
Add attributes (name, type) to each feature in the attribute table.
Use the measuring tool to find lengths and areas, and print or export a map with title, scale, key and north arrow.
practicals.expectedObservations: Each layer can be switched on or off; queries show features meeting a condition (e.g. all classrooms); the software computes areas and distances automatically.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Raster area: a land-use class covers 1250 cells of 30 m × 30 m. Area of one cell = 900 m². Total = 1250 × 900 = 1 125 000 m² = 112.5 ha = 1.125 km².
Scale check: a 100 m school fence digitised as 4.0 cm on screen at 1:2500 → 4.0 × 2500 = 10 000 cm = 100 m.
precautions: Set the correct coordinate system before digitising.
Save work regularly.
Check the accuracy of GPS points (wait for a good signal).
commonMistakes: Confusing raster (cells) with vector (points, lines, polygons) data.
Forgetting map elements: title, key, scale, north arrow.
Calling GIS only software.
examTips: List the components of GIS, sources of data (remote sensing, surveys, digitising, scanning, field work) and uses (defence, census, agriculture, urban planning).
Mention problems in Nigeria: power supply, cost, trained personnel.

checkQuestions.q: Which is NOT a component of GIS?
checkQuestions.explanation: GIS components are hardware, software, data, procedures and people.

checkQuestions.q: 200 raster cells of 10 m × 10 m cover an area of
Roads are best stored in a GIS as
checkQuestions.explanation: Roads are linear features.

practicals.title: Latitude and distance; longitude and time
practicals.aim: To calculate north–south distances from latitude and local time differences from longitude, and to illustrate them on a globe diagram.
materials: Table of places with latitudes and longitudes
safety: No special hazards.
procedure: Find the latitude and longitude of the places from an atlas.
For distance along a meridian, find the difference in latitude (subtract if on the same side of the equator, add if on opposite sides) and multiply by 111 km.
For time, find the difference in longitude (subtract if both east or both west, add if on opposite sides of Greenwich).
Convert degrees to time: 15° = 1 hour, 1° = 4 minutes.
Add time for places to the east; subtract for places to the west.
Draw a labelled diagram of the earth showing the lines used.
practicals.expectedObservations: Places east of a given point have later local times because the earth rotates from west to east.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Lagos is about 3°E, a place at 45°E: difference = 42° → 42 × 4 = 168 min = 2 h 48 min. When it is 12 noon in Lagos, it is 2:48 p.m. at 45°E.
A place at 30°W: difference from 3°E = 33° → 132 min = 2 h 12 min earlier → 9:48 a.m.
Latitude: Lagos 6.5°N, Kano 12°N → 5.5° × 111 km ≈ 610.5 km apart (north–south).
precautions: Check whether places are on the same or opposite sides of the prime meridian or equator.
Convert remaining minutes correctly (60 min = 1 h).
sourcesOfError: The 111 km value is an approximation.
commonMistakes: Subtracting time for places to the east.
Subtracting longitudes when places are on opposite sides of Greenwich.
Confusing local time with standard (zone) time.
examTips: Set out: difference in longitude → time difference → answer with a.m./p.m.
Explain that the earth rotates 360° in 24 hours, so 15° per hour.

checkQuestions.q: A longitude difference of 30° corresponds to a time difference of
When it is noon at 0°, the local time at 60°E is
checkQuestions.explanation: 60° = 4 hours ahead to the east.

practicals.title: The school weather station: Stevenson screen and thermometers
practicals.aim: To describe the siting of a Stevenson screen, read maximum and minimum and wet-and-dry bulb thermometers, and calculate daily mean temperature, range and relative humidity.
apparatus: Six's maximum and minimum thermometer (or separate maximum and minimum thermometers)
materials: Distilled water for the wet-bulb reservoir
safety: Handle glass thermometers carefully; report breakages so mercury can be cleaned up safely.
Do not lean on the screen's stand.
procedure: Inspect the Stevenson screen: white, louvred wooden box on legs about 1.2 m above short grass, door facing away from the sun, sited in the open away from buildings and trees.
At the same time each day (e.g. 9 a.m.), read the maximum and minimum temperatures at the bottom of each index.
Reset the indices with the magnet.
Read the dry-bulb and wet-bulb thermometers and calculate the wet-bulb depression.
Use the table to find relative humidity.
Record and calculate daily mean temperature and daily range; at the end of a week, find weekly means.
practicals.expectedObservations: Maximum temperatures occur in the early afternoon and minimum temperatures just before dawn. The wet bulb reads lower than the dry bulb because evaporation cools it; a small depression means high humidity.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Max 32 °C, min 22 °C → daily mean = (32 + 22) ÷ 2 = 27 °C; daily range = 32 − 22 = 10 °C.
Dry bulb 30 °C, wet bulb 26 °C → depression 4 °C → relative humidity ≈ 73% (from table).
Weekly maxima 31, 32, 33, 30, 32, 31, 31 °C → mean maximum = 220 ÷ 7 ≈ 31.4 °C.
precautions: Read thermometers at eye level to avoid parallax.
Keep the wet-bulb muslin clean and wet with distilled water.
Take readings at the same time daily.
sourcesOfError: Dirty or dry muslin on the wet bulb.
Screen placed too close to buildings.
commonMistakes: Reading the top instead of the bottom of the index in Six's thermometer.
Calculating range as max + min.
Saying the screen is painted white to look clean (it reflects sunlight).
examTips: Describe the screen's features with reasons: white to reflect heat, louvres for free air circulation, legs to avoid ground heat, door facing away from direct sun.
Name the instrument, what it measures and its unit.

checkQuestions.q: The Stevenson screen is painted white to
checkQuestions.explanation: Reflection prevents direct heating of the thermometers.

checkQuestions.q: A maximum of 34 °C and minimum of 24 °C give a daily range of
A large difference between dry- and wet-bulb readings indicates
checkQuestions.explanation: Rapid evaporation from the wet bulb occurs in dry air.

checkQuestions.q: In Six's thermometer, readings are taken from the
checkQuestions.explanation: The indices are pushed by the mercury and remain at the extremes.

practicals.title: Measuring rainfall, wind direction and wind speed
practicals.aim: To use a rain gauge, wind vane and anemometer, record daily observations and calculate rainfall totals and averages.
safety: Do not climb on roofs or poles to read instruments.
Avoid the station during thunderstorms.
procedure: Sink the rain gauge in open ground with its rim about 30 cm above the surface, away from trees and buildings.
Each morning at a fixed time, pour the collected water into the graduated cylinder and read the rainfall in mm at eye level.
Note the wind direction from the wind vane (the direction the wind blows FROM).
Count anemometer revolutions or read the dial for wind speed; estimate force with the Beaufort scale.
Read the barometer pressure in millibars.
Record daily data and compute weekly and monthly totals and means.
practicals.expectedObservations: During the rainy season most rain falls in heavy afternoon or evening storms; south-west winds dominate in the wet season and north-east (harmattan) winds in the dry season.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Daily rainfall in a week (mm): 0, 12, 25, 0, 8, 30, 5 → total = 80 mm; mean = 80 ÷ 7 ≈ 11.4 mm/day; rain days = 5.
Anemometer: cups on a circle of radius 0.15 m make 120 revolutions per minute → circumference = 2π × 0.15 ≈ 0.942 m → speed ≈ 0.942 × 120 ÷ 60 ≈ 1.9 m/s (approximate; real anemometers are calibrated).
precautions: Site the gauge in the open to avoid splash and shelter.
Read the measuring cylinder at eye level at the bottom of the meniscus.
Record at the same time each day.
sourcesOfError: Evaporation from the gauge in hot weather.
commonMistakes: Saying the wind vane points to where the wind is going.
Adding daily means instead of daily totals for monthly rainfall.
Confusing the barometer (pressure) with the hygrometer (humidity).
examTips: Draw and label a rain gauge: funnel, collecting jar, outer case, measuring cylinder.
Winds are named after the direction they blow from.

checkQuestions.q: A wind vane pointing towards the south-west shows a
checkQuestions.explanation: The arrow points into the wind, i.e. where it comes from.

checkQuestions.q: Rainfall of 10, 0, 15 and 5 mm on four days gives a total of
Atmospheric pressure is measured with a
checkQuestions.explanation: Barometers measure pressure in millibars.

practicals.title: Interpreting climatic data and drawing a climograph
practicals.aim: To plot monthly temperature (line) and rainfall (bars) on one graph and calculate annual mean temperature, annual range and total rainfall.
materials: Table of mean monthly temperature and rainfall for a station
safety: No special hazards.
procedure: Draw the horizontal axis with the 12 months (J–D).
Draw a left vertical axis for rainfall (mm) and a right vertical axis for temperature (°C) with suitable scales.
Draw rainfall as bars for each month.
Plot temperature as points at mid-month and join them with a smooth line.
Calculate annual total rainfall, annual mean temperature and annual range of temperature.
Describe the climate and identify the season pattern.
practicals.expectedObservations: A southern Nigerian station shows high temperatures throughout the year with a small range and two rainfall peaks; a northern station shows a single rainy season and a long dry season with a larger temperature range.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Station data, temperature (°C): 27, 28, 28, 28, 27, 26, 25, 25, 26, 26, 27, 27 → sum = 320, mean ≈ 26.7 °C; range = 28 − 25 = 3 °C.
Rainfall (mm): 25, 45, 100, 150, 270, 460, 270, 65, 140, 205, 70, 25 → total = 1825 mm.
Months with more than 100 mm: 6 (April–July, September, October), with peaks in June and October.
precautions: Use clearly different symbols and a key for rainfall and temperature.
Choose scales that fit the largest values.
Label both vertical axes with units.
commonMistakes: Calculating range as the difference between highest and lowest rainfall.
Adding temperatures and calling the sum the 'total'.
Plotting temperature as bars.
examTips: When identifying the climate, quote the data: e.g. 'annual range 3 °C, total 1825 mm, double maxima — equatorial/tropical wet'.
Annual range = highest monthly mean − lowest monthly mean.

checkQuestions.q: Highest monthly mean 32 °C and lowest 21 °C give an annual range of
On a climograph, rainfall is normally shown as
checkQuestions.explanation: Bars for rainfall, line for temperature.

checkQuestions.q: Twelve monthly temperatures totalling 330 °C give an annual mean of

practicals.title: Identifying climate types from data
practicals.aim: To use temperature and rainfall statistics to identify the climate type (equatorial, tropical continental/savanna, desert, Mediterranean, etc.) of a station and its hemisphere.
materials: Climatic tables for several unnamed stations
safety: No special hazards.
procedure: Calculate annual mean temperature, annual range and total rainfall for each station.
Note the months of maximum rainfall and the length of the dry season.
Decide the hemisphere from when the hottest months and the rainy season occur.
Compare the figures with the characteristics of each climate type.
Name the climate and give evidence from the figures.
practicals.expectedObservations: Equatorial: all months hot (about 27 °C), range below 3 °C, rain all year (over 1500 mm). Tropical continental: hot, range 5–10 °C, rainy season in summer, long dry season. Desert: very low rainfall (under 250 mm), large daily range. Mediterranean: winter rain and dry hot summers.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Station X: temperatures 22 °C (Jan) to 33 °C (May); rainfall total 750 mm, falling in June–September; dry season 7 months. Range = 33 − 22 = 11 °C → tropical continental (Sudan savanna) climate, Northern Hemisphere (rain in June–September).
Station Y: temperatures 26–28 °C, total 2400 mm, no month under 60 mm → equatorial.
precautions: Read the units carefully (mm vs cm).
Use all the evidence: range, total, seasonality.
sourcesOfError: Stations at high altitude have lower temperatures than expected for their latitude.
commonMistakes: Identifying a climate from temperature alone.
Forgetting to state the hemisphere when asked.
Calling every hot climate 'equatorial'.
examTips: Give at least three pieces of statistical evidence for the identification.
Know Köppen letters for the main types: Af (equatorial), Aw (tropical wet-and-dry), BW (desert), Cs (Mediterranean).

checkQuestions.q: A station with heavy rain in every month and an annual temperature range of 2 °C has
checkQuestions.explanation: These are typical equatorial features.

checkQuestions.q: Rain mainly in December–February with hottest months at the same time suggests the station is in the
checkQuestions.explanation: Summer (and summer rain) occurs in December–February south of the equator.

checkQuestions.q: Total annual rainfall below 250 mm indicates a
checkQuestions.explanation: Deserts receive very little rain.

practicals.title: Identifying common rocks
practicals.aim: To identify igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rock samples from their characteristics and test simple properties such as reaction with acid, hardness and density.
materials: Rock samples: granite, basalt, sandstone, shale, limestone, marble, quartzite, laterite
safety: Wear eye protection when using acid; rinse spills with water.
Scratch away from your body; do not hammer rocks without goggles.
procedure: Examine each rock with a hand lens for crystals, grains, layers, fossils and colour.
Scratch each rock with a steel nail to compare hardness.
Add a drop of dilute acid; record fizzing.
Weigh a rock sample, then find its volume by displacement in a measuring cylinder of water.
Calculate density = mass ÷ volume.
Classify each rock and state one use.
practicals.expectedObservations: Granite: coarse, interlocking crystals of quartz, feldspar and mica; hard (igneous intrusive). Basalt: dark, fine-grained (igneous extrusive). Sandstone: gritty grains, may show layers. Shale: fine layers that split easily. Limestone and marble fizz with acid; marble has sugary crystals. Quartzite: very hard, does not fizz.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Granite sample: mass 260 g; water level rises from 150 cm³ to 250 cm³ → volume 100 cm³. Density = 260 ÷ 100 = 2.6 g/cm³.
Basalt sample: 150 g, volume 50 cm³ → 3.0 g/cm³, denser than granite.
precautions: Use fresh surfaces for observation.
Rinse the rock after the acid test.
Read the measuring cylinder at eye level.
commonMistakes: Calling all layered rocks sedimentary — gneiss is banded metamorphic rock.
Confusing marble (metamorphic) with limestone (sedimentary).
Omitting the uses of rocks.
examTips: Give the rock type, mode of formation and an example of its location in Nigeria (e.g. granite in Jos Plateau, limestone at Ewekoro and Sokoto).
Relate rock characteristics to the landforms they produce (e.g. inselbergs on granite).

checkQuestions.q: A rock that fizzes with dilute acid is most likely
checkQuestions.explanation: Calcium carbonate reacts with acid to give carbon dioxide.

checkQuestions.q: A rock with 312 g mass and 120 cm³ volume has density
Marble is formed from limestone by
checkQuestions.explanation: Marble is metamorphosed limestone.

practicals.title: Population calculations: density, growth and pyramids
practicals.aim: To calculate population density, natural increase and doubling time, and to draw and interpret an age–sex pyramid.
safety: No special hazards.
procedure: Calculate population density = population ÷ area.
Calculate rate of natural increase = (birth rate − death rate) ÷ 10, as a percentage.
Estimate doubling time = 70 ÷ growth rate (%).
Draw an age–sex pyramid: horizontal bars for 5-year age groups, males left and females right, as percentages of the total population.
Describe the shape and explain what it shows about births, deaths and dependency.
Calculate the dependency ratio.
practicals.expectedObservations: Developing countries such as Nigeria show a broad-based, triangular pyramid (high birth rates, many young dependants); developed countries show narrower bases and wider tops.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Birth rate 38 per 1000, death rate 12 per 1000 → natural increase = 26 per 1000 = 2.6% per year. Doubling time ≈ 70 ÷ 2.6 ≈ 27 years.
Dependency ratio: aged 0–14 = 43%, 65+ = 3%, 15–64 = 54% → (43 + 3) ÷ 54 × 100 ≈ 85.2 dependants per 100 workers.
Density: 2 400 000 people in 12 000 km² → 200 per km².
precautions: Use percentages for pyramids so countries can be compared.
Keep bars of equal height for each age group.
sourcesOfError: Inaccurate census data, especially age reporting.
commonMistakes: Confusing birth rate per 1000 with percentage.
Placing males on the right.
Ignoring migration when explaining population change.
examTips: Explain the factors behind the pattern (fertility, health care, migration).
State the implications: e.g. a youthful population needs more schools and jobs.

checkQuestions.q: Birth rate 40 and death rate 15 per 1000 give a natural increase of
A population growing at 3.5% a year doubles in about
A broad-based population pyramid indicates
checkQuestions.explanation: Many young children result from high fertility.

practicals.title: Field work: land-use survey along a transect
practicals.aim: To survey and map rural or urban land use along a transect in the school locality, present the data and explain the pattern.
apparatus: Base map or sketch map of the area
Measuring tape (30 m) or pacing record
materials: Land-use classification key (e.g. residential, commercial, industrial, farmland, open space, institutional)
safety: Work in groups with a teacher's permission and a letter of introduction where needed.
Keep away from moving traffic; stand on the pavement or verge and wear bright clothing.
Be polite to residents and traders; respect privacy and do not record names without consent.
procedure: Choose a topic and hypothesis, e.g. 'Commercial land use decreases with distance from the market'.
Plan a transect line on the base map from the centre outward and divide it into equal sections (e.g. 50 m).
Walk the transect, recording the dominant land use on each side of each section with the key.
Measure the length of each land-use type along the transect.
Transfer the data to a land-use map with colours and a key; draw a bar graph or pie chart.
Analyse the pattern, test the hypothesis and write a report: introduction, methods, results, discussion, conclusion and problems encountered.
practicals.expectedObservations: Commercial uses (shops, banks, market stalls) dominate near the town centre; residential uses increase outwards; farmland and open space appear at the edge.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Transect of 1000 m: commercial 350 m, residential 400 m, institutional 100 m, farmland 150 m.
Percentages: commercial 35%, residential 40%, institutional 10%, farmland 15%.
Pie-chart angles: 126°, 144°, 36°, 54° (total 360°).
precautions: Use a clear, agreed classification key.
Record data immediately on the sheet.
Visit at a time when uses are visible (e.g. market day noted).
sourcesOfError: Mixed land use in one building (shop below, home above).
Personal judgement in classifying land uses.
commonMistakes: No hypothesis or aim.
Presenting raw data only without maps or diagrams.
Conclusions not linked to the data collected.
examTips: Field work is assessed by the school (continuous assessment); a well-structured report with aim, methods, results, analysis and conclusion earns most marks.
Be ready to describe the methods and problems of field work in Paper 3 questions.

checkQuestions.q: Residential land along 450 m of a 1500 m transect is
The first step in a field work project is to
checkQuestions.explanation: An aim or hypothesis guides data collection.

checkQuestions.q: A transect is
options: a line along which observations are made at intervals
checkQuestions.explanation: Transects allow systematic sampling across an area.

practicals.title: Field work: market survey and traffic count
practicals.aim: To carry out a market survey (goods, origins of traders) and a traffic flow count at a road junction, and present the results.
materials: Classification of vehicles (cars, buses, motorcycles, trucks, tricycles)
safety: Work in groups with a teacher's permission and a letter of introduction where needed.
Keep away from moving traffic; stand on the pavement or verge and wear bright clothing.
Be polite to residents and traders; respect privacy and do not record names without consent.
procedure: Design a short questionnaire for traders: goods sold, where goods come from, distance travelled, mode of transport.
Interview a sample of traders (e.g. every fifth stall) and record answers.
For traffic flow, choose a safe count point at a junction.
Count vehicles by type in each direction for 15-minute periods at morning peak, midday and evening peak.
Convert counts to vehicles per hour and draw bar graphs and a flow map.
Analyse the results and draw conclusions about the market's sphere of influence and traffic peaks.
practicals.expectedObservations: Most foodstuffs come from nearby villages while manufactured goods come from larger cities; traffic peaks in the morning and evening when people travel to and from work and school; motorcycles and tricycles dominate on local roads.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Traffic count in 15 min (morning): cars 45, motorcycles 80, buses 20, trucks 5 → total 150 → 150 × 4 = 600 vehicles per hour.
Motorcycles = 80 ÷ 150 × 100 ≈ 53.3%.
Market survey: 24 of 40 traders came from within 10 km → 60%.
precautions: Use a systematic sample of traders to avoid bias.
Count at the same times and for the same durations.
Use tally marks in groups of five.
commonMistakes: Counting for unequal periods and comparing totals directly.
Asking leading or too many questions.
No map of the study area.
examTips: Explain why sampling is needed and how it was done.
Present results with appropriate diagrams: bar graphs for counts, flow maps for directions.

checkQuestions.q: 120 vehicles counted in 15 minutes is a rate of
checkQuestions.explanation: 120 × 4 = 480 per hour.

checkQuestions.q: Interviewing every fifth trader is an example of
checkQuestions.explanation: A fixed interval is systematic sampling.

checkQuestions.q: Traffic counts are usually highest
checkQuestions.explanation: Journeys to and from work and school concentrate at these times.

practicals.title: Field work: measuring the rate of soil erosion
practicals.aim: To measure the rate of soil erosion on bare and vegetated slopes in the locality using erosion pins (pegs) and relate it to slope and cover.
apparatus: Metal or wooden pins (pegs) 30 cm long
safety: Choose slopes that are safe to walk on; avoid gully edges.
Get permission from the landowner.
Wear covered shoes; watch for snakes.
procedure: Select two plots of equal size on similar slopes: one bare, one grassed.
Measure the slope angle with the clinometer.
Drive 10 pins into each plot in a grid so that exactly 10 cm stands above the surface; record the exposed length.
Measure the exposed length of each pin after each month of the rainy season.
Calculate the mean loss of soil depth and the rate per month.
Present the results as a line graph and explain the differences.
practicals.expectedObservations: Pins on the bare plot become more exposed than those on the grassed plot; erosion is fastest after heavy storms and on steeper slopes; rills may form on bare ground.
practicals.dataAndCalculations:
Bare plot: mean exposure increased from 10.0 cm to 13.2 cm in 8 months → loss = 3.2 cm → rate = 3.2 ÷ 8 = 0.4 cm per month.
Grassed plot: 10.0 → 10.4 cm → 0.4 cm in 8 months = 0.05 cm per month. Bare-plot erosion is 0.4 ÷ 0.05 = 8 times faster.
Volume of soil lost from a 10 m × 10 m bare plot = 100 m² × 0.032 m = 3.2 m³.
precautions: Hammer pins vertically and to the same initial height.
Measure from the same side of each pin.
Take readings at the same intervals.
sourcesOfError: Pins disturbed by people or animals.
Measurement to the nearest mm only.
commonMistakes: Not having a control (vegetated) plot.
Using unequal plot sizes or slopes.
Explaining results without reference to rainfall.
examTips: Link findings to causes (rainfall intensity, slope, vegetation cover, human activity) and control measures (cover crops, terraces, contour ploughing, afforestation).
Show the rate calculation with units.

checkQuestions.q: Pin exposure increases by 1.8 cm in 6 months. The rate of erosion is
checkQuestions.explanation: 1.8 ÷ 6 = 0.3 cm per month.

checkQuestions.q: Why is a grassed plot also studied?
options: Because bare plots cannot be measured
checkQuestions.explanation: It shows the effect of vegetation cover on erosion.

checkQuestions.q: Which measure reduces erosion on slopes?
checkQuestions.explanation: Terraces and cover reduce runoff speed.
